theory.question: Distinguish schema-on-read from schema-on-write.
theory.answer:
Schema-on-write is analogous to static type checking: the database catches missing or wrongly typed fields at insert time, every row is guaranteed to have the expected columns, and queries can assume a uniform structure. Adding a new column requires a migration (ALTER TABLE + UPDATE), which on large tables can mean minutes of downtime (MySQL copies the entire table) or a carefully orchestrated online migration.

Schema-on-read is analogous to dynamic type checking: new fields can be added to new documents without touching old ones, and application code handles both shapes. This is advantageous when different objects have genuinely different structures, when the schema is determined by an external system you do not control, or when the schema is evolving rapidly and migrations are costly.

Comment: PostgreSQL JSONB gives you both: a relational table (schema-on-write) with a JSONB column inside it (schema-on-read) for flexible attributes.

theory.question: Explain why normalization uses IDs instead of duplicating human-readable strings.
theory.answer:
In practice: if you store 'Greater Seattle Area' as a plain string in 10,000 user rows and the region is renamed, you need a bulk UPDATE touching every one of those rows. If you store a region_id foreign key and keep the name in a single regions table, one UPDATE on one row propagates everywhere automatically.

Normalization naturally produces many-to-one relationships (many users → one region), which require joins at read time. Document databases handle this poorly since joins are weak or absent, forcing a choice between denormalization (with its consistency risk) or multiple round-trips in application code.

theory.question: Describe when the document model breaks down and when it is appropriate to use.
theory.answer:
Imperative vs. declarative — the core difference:
An imperative query language (e.g., a for-loop in application code, or the old MongoDB query API) tells the database or runtime exactly how to find the data: iterate through these records, check this condition, collect the matches. The sequence of steps is fixed by the programmer.
A declarative query language (SQL, CSS, Datalog) describes only what the result should look like. The system — database engine or browser — decides how to produce it: which index to use, in what order to scan, whether to parallelize.

A CSS comparison makes this concrete: CSS declaratively selects elements by pattern and applies styles; the browser handles invalidation automatically. Equivalent imperative JavaScript must manually remove styles when conditions change, and must be rewritten to use new browser APIs. SQL has the same property — adding an index does not require changing any query.

For daily work: when you write application code that iterates over rows and filters them in memory, you are writing an imperative query. That bypasses the optimizer, disables indexes, and pulls data over the network unnecessarily. If the filter can be expressed in SQL, it should be.

theory.question: Describe data locality (how data is stored physically) in document storage and when it matters.
theory.answer:
In a normalized relational schema, rendering a user profile requires joining users, positions, education, and contact tables — multiple index lookups and potentially multiple disk seeks. In a document store, the whole profile is one blob, loaded in a single read.

Locality is not unique to document databases. Google Spanner allows table rows to be interleaved within a parent table. Oracle has multi-table index cluster tables. Cassandra and HBase use column families. The principle is the same: group data that is accessed together, physically together.

Comment: Locality matters most when documents map directly to a single UI view and are loaded atomically. It matters less for analytical queries that only touch a few fields across many rows.

theory.question: You have a User object in your application code with nested lists: a list of job positions and a list of education entries. Describe what problems arise when you store and reload this object using a relational database, and how a document database handles it differently.
theory.answer:
The concrete problem: a User object in application code has a list of positions and a list of education entries. In a relational database, those become separate tables linked by foreign keys. Every read requires joining them back together; every write requires coordinated inserts across multiple tables. ORM frameworks like ActiveRecord and Hibernate reduce the boilerplate but cannot fully hide the mismatch — the N+1 query problem, eager vs. lazy loading decisions, and migration coordination all leak through.

Document databases reduce this friction for entities that are naturally tree-shaped and loaded in full. A résumé as a JSON document maps closely to the object in memory: one fetch, one object, no translation. The mismatch reappears as soon as the entity grows relationships to other entities (company pages, recommendations) that cannot be embedded.

For daily engineering, the practical implication is: evaluate your most common read pattern first. If it always loads the full entity, a document model or a JSONB column may simplify your code. If you frequently query subsets of fields across many rows, the relational model wins.

theory.question: Explain what's the difference between declarative and imperative query languages and why declarative query languages like SQL outperform imperative query APIs.
theory.answer:
A CSS comparison makes this concrete: CSS declaratively selects elements by pattern and applies styles; the browser handles invalidation automatically. Equivalent imperative JavaScript must manually remove styles when conditions change, and must be rewritten to use new browser APIs. SQL has the same property — adding an index does not require changing any query.

For daily work: when you write application code that iterates over rows and filters them in memory, you are writing an imperative query. That bypasses the optimizer, disables indexes, and pulls data over the network unnecessarily. If the filter can be expressed in SQL, it should be.

theory.question: PostgreSQL added a JSON column type; MongoDB added a SQL-like aggregation pipeline. What does this tell you about the long-term direction of relational vs. document databases, and what does it mean for picking a database for a new project?
theory.answer:
On the relational side: PostgreSQL (since 9.3), MySQL (since 5.7), and IBM DB2 (since 10.5) support JSON columns with querying and indexing inside the JSON. This lets relational databases store heterogeneous, schema-on-read data in a single column while keeping the surrounding schema strict.

On the document side: RethinkDB supports relational-like joins in its query language. Some MongoDB drivers automatically resolve database references, effectively performing a client-side join. MongoDB added the aggregation pipeline — a declarative query language that resembles SQL, showing that NoSQL systems tend to reinvent relational concepts over time.

For practical architecture decisions, convergence means you often do not need to choose between relational and document: PostgreSQL with JSONB gives you both in one system. Fully normalized tables for entities with stable structure and many-to-many relationships; JSONB columns for flexible attributes, heterogeneous event payloads, or external data whose shape you do not control. This reduces operational overhead compared to running two separate database systems.

theory.question: A financial ledger must reconstruct any past account balance and explain every adjustment. Decide whether event sourcing fits this use case, and describe the problems it introduces.
theory.answer:
Event sourcing fits when the history of changes is as important as the current state. Instead of overwriting an account balance, the system appends immutable domain events such as `MoneyDeposited`, `PaymentAuthorized`, and `ChargeReversed`; the current balance is a projection derived by processing those events in order. This provides a durable audit trail, supports temporal queries, and lets the team rebuild a broken projection or create a new read model from the same history. It is also useful for version control, inventory movements, and workflows where knowing why state changed matters.

"Event Sourcing ensures that all changes to application state are stored as a sequence of events." — Martin Fowler

The cost is substantial operational and application complexity. Replaying a long stream can be slow, so systems need snapshots and carefully versioned projections. Event schemas must remain readable for years; renaming a field or changing business rules may require upcasters, migration events, or compatibility code. Concurrent writers need an ordering or optimistic-concurrency rule, and consumers must be idempotent because delivery can be retried. Read models are derived asynchronously in many designs, so a user may briefly see stale data after a successful write. Replays must not repeat external side effects such as charging a card or sending an email. Incorrect facts are normally corrected with compensating events rather than deleting history, which can conflict with privacy or deletion requirements.

For ordinary CRUD systems that only need the latest state, these costs usually outweigh the audit and replay benefits. A conventional transactional database plus an audit log is simpler unless event history is genuinely the source of truth.

Comment: Martin Fowler's original description covers reconstruction, temporal queries, and replay: https://www.martinfowler.com/eaaDev/EventSourcing.html

practice.task: [Kafka, PostgreSQL, MongoDB] Compare precomputed read models with a native materialized view.
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ with a compatible Docker Compose CLI plugin that supports `docker compose up --wait`, or Docker Desktop with that capability.

This lab uses an Apache Kafka 4.2 topic as the append-only order event log. A Python projector replays that log into application-maintained precomputed read models: ordinary `orders_view` and `daily_revenue_view` tables in PostgreSQL 16 and a `customer_spend_view` collection in MongoDB 8. This is analogous to Twitter-style precomputed per-user timelines, where application logic maintains data shaped for fast reads. The lab also builds `daily_revenue_materialized` as a separate native PostgreSQL materialized view over `orders_view`, so you can compare explicit incremental table updates with a database-stored query result refreshed on demand. The stack initializes topic `order-events` with the four events below, the two empty PostgreSQL projection tables, and an empty MongoDB collection plus unique index; you create the native materialized view during the exercise.

Setup:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch3-p1 init
docker compose up -d --wait
```

:::cut Observe the current state

```bash
ls -l
```

Expected lab files: `docker-compose.yml`, `initial_order_events.txt`, `mongo_views.js`, `new_order_event.txt`, `postgres_views.sql`, `projector.py`, `revenue_materialized_view.sql`, and `test_projector.py`.

The Kafka topic is pre-seeded with these keyed records (`key|json`):

```
o1|{"event_id":"evt-001","event_type":"OrderPlaced","order_id":"o1","customer_id":"alice","total":100,"day":"2026-08-01"}
o2|{"event_id":"evt-002","event_type":"OrderPlaced","order_id":"o2","customer_id":"alice","total":50,"day":"2026-08-01"}
o3|{"event_id":"evt-003","event_type":"OrderPlaced","order_id":"o3","customer_id":"bob","total":70,"day":"2026-08-02"}
o2|{"event_id":"evt-004","event_type":"OrderCancelled","order_id":"o2","customer_id":"alice","total":50,"day":"2026-08-01"}
```

`new_order_event.txt` contains the extra event you append later:

```
o4|{"event_id":"evt-005","event_type":"OrderPlaced","order_id":"o4","customer_id":"alice","total":30,"day":"2026-08-02"}
```

PostgreSQL database `order_views` starts with empty projection tables:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders_view (
  order_id    TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('placed', 'cancelled')),
  total       INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (total >= 0),
  day         DATE NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE daily_revenue_view (
  day         DATE PRIMARY KEY,
  net_revenue INTEGER NOT NULL
);
```

MongoDB database `order_views` starts with an empty `customer_spend_view` collection and a unique index on `customer_id`:

```javascript
db.createCollection('customer_spend_view');
db.customer_spend_view.createIndex({ customer_id: 1 }, { unique: true });
```
:::

1. Implement `read_events`. Create a Confluent Kafka consumer with auto-commit disabled, read partition 0's low and high watermarks, assign the low offset explicitly, and poll exactly `high - low` records in offset order. Decode each JSON value, fail on Kafka errors or a ten-second timeout, and close the consumer even on failure.


6. In 7–10 sentences, compare the ordinary `daily_revenue_view` table, whose totals the projector updates incrementally, with the native `daily_revenue_materialized` view, whose stored query result PostgreSQL replaces only when explicitly refreshed. Relate the ordinary precomputed read models to Twitter-style per-user timelines. Also explain why Kafka is authoritative while every read model is disposable, why retention must preserve all events needed for a rebuild, why one partition gives total order but limits parallelism, and why PostgreSQL and MongoDB writes are not one atomic transaction. Mention how event IDs, checkpoints, idempotent writes, or versioned replacement projections support recovery.
7. Tear down the Docker stack with `docker compose down -v`.

practice.task: [GraphQL.js, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Neo4j] Learn how to unify multiple data stores behind one typed API.
[PostgreSQL, OrientDB] Compare recursive SQL with graph traversal for package dependencies.
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop).

Use the same directed package graph in PostgreSQL and OrientDB to resolve every dependency of `myapp` and find every package affected by a breaking change to `utils`. The lab image supplies a Docker Compose stack, seeded databases, two query scaffolds, and a verification script.

Setup:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch3-p3 init
docker compose up -d --wait
```

:::cut Inspect the schema, seed graph, and starter files
Run:

```bash
ls -l
ls -l preloaded_data
```

After `init` completes, these lab files are available: `docker-compose.yml`, `postgres_compare.sql`, `orient_compare.osql`, and `verify_queries.sh`. The seed files are visible under `preloaded_data/` as `postgres_seed.sql` and `orient_seed.osql`.

PostgreSQL uses `packages(id, name, version)` and `deps(package_id, depends_on_id)`. OrientDB represents the same data as `Package` vertices joined by directed `DEPENDS_ON` edges.

The seeded edges are `myapp` → `webserver`, `myapp` → `logger`, `webserver` → `router`, `webserver` → `logger`, `router` → `http-lib`, `router` → `crypto`, and `logger` → `utils`.

`postgres_compare.sql` contains two incomplete recursive CTEs: `all_deps(dep_id, depth, path)` and `impacted(pkg_id, depth, path)`. Their final queries already join package names and versions, reduce duplicate visits with `MIN(depth)`, and order by hop count and name.

`orient_compare.osql` connects to `remote:localhost/demodb` as `admin` and contains markers for the forward and reverse traversals.
:::

:::cut View the query scaffolds
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE all_deps(dep_id, depth, path) AS (
  -- implement: direct dependencies
  SELECT NULL::INT, NULL::INT, ARRAY[]::INT[]
  WHERE FALSE
  UNION ALL
  -- implement: recursive outbound traversal with cycle guard
  SELECT NULL::INT, NULL::INT, ARRAY[]::INT[]
  FROM all_deps ad
  WHERE FALSE
)
SELECT p.name, p.version, MIN(ad.depth) AS min_hops
FROM all_deps ad
JOIN packages p ON p.id = ad.dep_id
GROUP BY p.name, p.version
ORDER BY min_hops, p.name;
```

```sql
CONNECT remote:localhost/demodb admin admin

-- implement: forward dependency traversal

-- implement: reverse impact traversal
```
:::

Tasks:

1. Complete the first PostgreSQL recursive CTE in `postgres_compare.sql`. Its base case must select direct dependencies of `myapp` at depth 1 and initialize an integer path containing the root and dependency IDs. Its recursive term must follow outbound edges, increment depth, append the next ID, and reject IDs already in the current path. Return every reachable package with its minimum hop count.

2. Complete the second PostgreSQL recursive CTE by following incoming edges from `utils`. Use the same path-based cycle guard and return every affected package with its minimum distance from `utils`.

3. Complete both queries in `orient_compare.osql`. For the forward query, start at the `Package` named `myapp`, traverse `DEPENDS_ON` edges with `out('DEPENDS_ON')`, use `MAXDEPTH 3` and `STRATEGY BREADTH_FIRST`, exclude the root, and return `$depth AS min_hops`, `name`, and `version` ordered by hop count and name. For the reverse query, start at `utils`, traverse with `in('DEPENDS_ON')`, apply the same depth, strategy, root exclusion, and ordering, and name the hop column `hops_from_utils`.

4. Run both completed query files through the containerized clients:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec -T postgres psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d lab < postgres_compare.sql
   docker compose exec -T orientdb /orientdb/bin/console.sh /lab/orient_compare.osql
   ```

5. Run the tests; the supplied script executes both query files through Docker Compose and asserts their observable results:

   ```bash
   bash verify_queries.sh
   ```

6. Compare the query shapes in 4–7 sentences. Map PostgreSQL's base case, recursive term, join direction, path guard, and `MIN(depth)` reduction to OrientDB's `out()` or `in()`, `MAXDEPTH`, and `BREADTH_FIRST`; then state when keeping the relationships in PostgreSQL is reasonable and when a graph database becomes clearer.

7. Tear down the Docker stack with `docker compose down -v`.
practice.answer:
postgres_compare.sql:
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE all_deps(dep_id, depth, path) AS (
  SELECT d.depends_on_id, 1, ARRAY[p.id, d.depends_on_id]
  FROM packages p
  JOIN deps d ON d.package_id = p.id
  WHERE p.name = 'myapp'

  UNION ALL

  SELECT d.depends_on_id, ad.depth + 1, ad.path || d.depends_on_id
  FROM all_deps ad
  JOIN deps d ON d.package_id = ad.dep_id
  WHERE NOT d.depends_on_id = ANY (ad.path)
)
SELECT p.name, p.version, MIN(ad.depth) AS min_hops
FROM all_deps ad
JOIN packages p ON p.id = ad.dep_id
GROUP BY p.name, p.version
ORDER BY min_hops, p.name;

WITH RECURSIVE impacted(pkg_id, depth, path) AS (
  SELECT d.package_id, 1, ARRAY[p.id, d.package_id]
  FROM packages p
  JOIN deps d ON d.depends_on_id = p.id
  WHERE p.name = 'utils'

  UNION ALL

  SELECT d.package_id, i.depth + 1, i.path || d.package_id
  FROM impacted i
  JOIN deps d ON d.depends_on_id = i.pkg_id
  WHERE NOT d.package_id = ANY (i.path)
)
SELECT p.name, p.version, MIN(i.depth) AS hops_from_utils
FROM impacted i
JOIN packages p ON p.id = i.pkg_id
GROUP BY p.name, p.version
ORDER BY hops_from_utils, p.name;
```

orient_compare.osql:
```sql
CONNECT remote:localhost/demodb admin admin
SELECT $depth AS min_hops, name, version FROM (TRAVERSE out('DEPENDS_ON') FROM (SELECT FROM Package WHERE name = 'myapp') MAXDEPTH 3 STRATEGY BREADTH_FIRST) WHERE $depth > 0 ORDER BY $depth, name
SELECT $depth AS hops_from_utils, name, version FROM (TRAVERSE in('DEPENDS_ON') FROM (SELECT FROM Package WHERE name = 'utils') MAXDEPTH 3 STRATEGY BREADTH_FIRST) WHERE $depth > 0 ORDER BY $depth, name
```

The PostgreSQL base case is the direct-edge join from the named root, while its recursive term repeatedly joins `deps` from the previous result. Forward resolution joins `package_id` to the current package and maps to OrientDB `out('DEPENDS_ON')`; reverse impact joins `depends_on_id` to the current package and maps to `in('DEPENDS_ON')`. PostgreSQL's integer `path` plus `ANY(path)` check prevents revisiting a vertex, whereas these bounded OrientDB traversals use `MAXDEPTH 3` and `BREADTH_FIRST` to produce shallow levels first. The final PostgreSQL `MIN(depth)` collapses duplicate paths to each package; the OrientDB graph's breadth-first traversal exposes its distance as `$depth`. Keeping relationships in PostgreSQL is reasonable when dependency queries are bounded and benefit from relational joins, transactions, and existing SQL tooling; a graph database becomes clearer when traversal-oriented queries and relationship navigation are dominant.

practice.task: [SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL] Learn how to detect and eliminate ORM N+1 queries.
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop).

This lab starts PostgreSQL 16 and a companion Python container with SQLAlchemy 2.0 and Psycopg 3. The generated `n_plus_one.py` maps the existing tables and leaves three relationship-loading strategies for you to implement.

Setup:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch3-p4 init
docker compose up -d --wait
```

:::cut Observe the current state
Inspect the generated files and the pre-seeded author and book counts:

```bash
ls -l
docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U postgres -d n1_lab -c "SELECT a.name, count(b.id) AS books FROM authors a LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id GROUP BY a.id ORDER BY a.id;"
```

Expected lab files: `docker-compose.yml` and `n_plus_one.py`.

The pre-seeded PostgreSQL schema and rows are:

```sql
CREATE TABLE authors (
  id   INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE books (
  id        INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  author_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES authors(id),
  title     TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO authors (name) VALUES
  ('Alice'),
  ('Bob'),
  ('Carol'),
  ('Dan');

INSERT INTO books (author_id, title)
SELECT id, 'Data Systems' FROM authors WHERE name = 'Alice'
UNION ALL
SELECT id, 'Reliable APIs' FROM authors WHERE name = 'Alice'
UNION ALL
SELECT id, 'Python Services' FROM authors WHERE name = 'Bob'
UNION ALL
SELECT id, 'Graph Thinking' FROM authors WHERE name = 'Carol'
UNION ALL
SELECT id, 'RDF in Practice' FROM authors WHERE name = 'Carol'
UNION ALL
SELECT id, 'Query Languages' FROM authors WHERE name = 'Carol';
```
:::

Tasks:

1. Implement `load_lazy`. Select all four `Author` objects ordered by ID, serialize the result yourself, and return the count with the rows. The rows must be a `list[tuple[str, list[str]]]`: each tuple contains the author's name followed by a list of that author's book titles. Preserve author ID order and the relationship's book ID order.
2. Implement `load_joined` by selecting all `Author` rows ordered by `Author.id` with `joinedload(Author.books)`. Deduplicate the ORM result before calling `all()`, then return the count with the rows (the same format as in task 1).
3. Implement `load_selectin` by selecting all `Author` rows ordered by `Author.id` with `selectinload(Author.books)`, then return the count with the rows (the same format as in task 1).
4. Run the tests:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec -T app python n_plus_one.py
   ```

5. In 3–5 sentences, compare joined eager loading with select-in loading. Explain why a joined collection repeats parent columns, when its single round trip is useful, and why select-in loading can be safer for large one-to-many collections.
6. Tear down the Docker stack with `docker compose down -v`.
practice.answer:
```python
def serialize(authors: list[Author]) -> list[tuple[str, list[str]]]:
    return [(author.name, [book.title for book in author.books]) for author in authors]


def load_lazy() -> tuple[int, list[tuple[str, list[str]]]]:
    global select_count
    select_count = 0
    with Session(engine) as session:
        authors = session.scalars(select(Author).order_by(Author.id)).all()
        rows = serialize(authors)
    return select_count, rows


def load_joined() -> tuple[int, list[tuple[str, list[str]]]]:
    global select_count
    select_count = 0
    with Session(engine) as session:
        statement = select(Author).options(joinedload(Author.books)).order_by(Author.id)
        authors = session.execute(statement).unique().scalars().all()
        rows = serialize(authors)
    return select_count, rows


def load_selectin() -> tuple[int, list[tuple[str, list[str]]]]:
    global select_count
    select_count = 0
    with Session(engine) as session:
        statement = select(Author).options(selectinload(Author.books)).order_by(Author.id)
        authors = session.scalars(statement).all()
        rows = serialize(authors)
    return select_count, rows
```

Joined eager loading retrieves parents and their collection rows in one query, but each book row repeats its author's columns. That single round trip is useful when collections are small or network latency makes additional queries costly. Select-in loading issues a parent query plus a second query for all matching child rows, avoiding the large joined result set that can be safer for sizeable one-to-many collections.

practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop).

This lab contrasts schema-on-write with schema-on-read by adding a typed relational field and evolving JSONB documents in PostgreSQL 16.

`notif_relational` demonstrates schema-on-write: PostgreSQL checks each row against declared columns and constraints when it is written, so introducing `priority` requires an `ALTER TABLE`, and every row receives the field. `notif_document` is a hybrid: its outer relational columns are still schema-on-write, while the keys inside `payload` demonstrate schema-on-read. PostgreSQL validates that `payload` contains valid JSONB at write time, but JSONB does not, by default, require every document to have the same keys or value types. Therefore `priority` and `ttl_seconds` may exist in only some payloads without a table migration; each query decides at read time how to interpret a missing key, for example as `'normal'` with `COALESCE` or as SQL `NULL`.

Setup:

```bash
docker run -d --name lab-ch3-p5 ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch3-p5
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch3-p5 init
```

:::cut Observe the starting schemas, seed data, and scaffold
The container starts with the following tables and rows. The `init` command also copies this SQL to `preloaded_data/seed.sql` so you can inspect the preload before working. Schema creation and seed inserts stay inside the image; do not recreate the tables.

```sql
CREATE TABLE notif_relational (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    INT  NOT NULL,
  type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  message    TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE notif_document (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    INT  NOT NULL,
  type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  payload    JSONB NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

INSERT INTO notif_relational (user_id, type, message) VALUES
  (1, 'email', 'Your order #1042 has shipped'),
  (2, 'push',  'Flash sale: 40% off electronics'),
  (3, 'sms',   'Your verification code is 8271'),
  (1, 'push',  'Your package was delivered');

INSERT INTO notif_document (user_id, type, payload) VALUES
  (1, 'email', '{"message": "Your order #1042 has shipped", "to": "alice@example.com", "subject": "Order update"}'),
  (2, 'push',  '{"message": "Flash sale: 40% off electronics", "device_token": "tok_abc", "badge": 1}'),
  (3, 'sms',   '{"message": "Your verification code is 8271", "phone": "+49123456789", "priority": "high"}'),
  (1, 'push',  '{"message": "Your package was delivered", "device_token": "tok_abc", "badge": 2}');
```

```bash
ls -l
cat preloaded_data/seed.sql
```

Expected lab files: `setup.sql`, `verify.sql`, and `preloaded_data/seed.sql`.
:::

Tasks:

1. Schema-on-write: Complete the relational sections in `setup.sql`. Add a text column named `priority` to `notif_relational`. Make the column required and give it a default value of `normal`. Set `priority` to `high` for every row whose `type` is `sms`. Finish with a query that returns `id`, `user_id`, `type`, `message`, `priority`, and `created_at`.
2. Schema-on-read: Complete the document priority projection without adding columns to `notif_document`. Select `id`, `type`, the `message` key from `payload` as `message`, and the `priority` key as `priority`; use `COALESCE` so a missing priority is returned as `'normal'`.
3. JSONB evolution under schema-on-read: Complete the JSONB evolution sections. For the existing rows whose `type` is `push`, merge a new payload field named `ttl_seconds` with the numeric value `86400`, using PostgreSQL's JSONB `||` operator. Insert one push row for user `2`. In its payload, store `New message from Sarah` under `message`, `tok_xyz` under `device_token`, the number `3` under `badge`, and the number `3600` under `ttl_seconds`. Finish with a projection of every document that returns `type`, exposes the payload's `message` field as `message`, and exposes its `ttl_seconds` field as `ttl`. JSONB permits this field to be added only to relevant documents without altering the table; readers must tolerate documents that do not contain it.

4. Apply the completed script and inspect its `SELECT` output:

   ```bash
   docker exec -i lab-ch3-p5 psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d lab < setup.sql
   ```

5. Run the tests:

   ```bash
   docker exec -i lab-ch3-p5 psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d lab < verify.sql
   ```

6. Tear down the Docker lab with `docker rm -f lab-ch3-p5`.
practice.answer:
```sql
ALTER TABLE notif_relational
  ADD COLUMN priority TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'normal';

UPDATE notif_relational
SET priority = 'high'
WHERE type = 'sms';

SELECT id, user_id, type, message, priority, created_at
FROM notif_relational;

SELECT
  id,
  type,
  payload ->> 'message' AS message,
  COALESCE(payload ->> 'priority', 'normal') AS priority
FROM notif_document;

UPDATE notif_document
SET payload = payload || '{"ttl_seconds": 86400}'::jsonb
WHERE type = 'push';

INSERT INTO notif_document (user_id, type, payload)
VALUES (
  2,
  'push',
  '{"message": "New message from Sarah", "device_token": "tok_xyz", "badge": 3, "ttl_seconds": 3600}'::jsonb
);

SELECT
  type,
  payload ->> 'message' AS message,
  payload ->> 'ttl_seconds' AS ttl
FROM notif_document;
```

The relational table enforces the new required priority column at write time. JSONB permits priority and ttl_seconds to vary by document, so readers use COALESCE for missing priority and tolerate NULL ttl values.

practice.task: [MongoDB] Learn how to join collections with an aggregation pipeline.
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop).

This lab starts MongoDB 8 and a companion Python container with PyMongo 4.17. The image-managed database initialization creates and seeds the `customers` and `orders` collections; `init` copies the exercise scaffold.

```bash
docker compose up -d --wait
```

:::cut Observe the current state
Inspect the generated scaffold:

```bash
ls -l
```

Expected lab files: `docker-compose.yml` and `document_lookup.py`.

The pre-seeded MongoDB `shop` database contains these representative documents; order `1005` deliberately refers to missing customer `99` so the aggregation can demonstrate left-join behavior. The initialization also creates a compound index on `orders.status` and `orders.total`.

```json
{

    { "_id": 1002, "customer_id": 2, "status": "pending", "total": 90 },
    { "_id": 1003, "customer_id": 1, "status": "paid", "total": 75 },
```

Tasks:

1. Build `pipeline` with a `$match` stage that keeps orders whose `status` is `paid` and whose `total` is at least 50. Follow it with `$lookup` from `customers`, matching the order's `customer_id` (`localField`) to the customer's `_id` (`foreignField`) and writing matches to `customer`.
2. Add `$unwind` for the `customer` array with `preserveNullAndEmptyArrays` set to `true`. Project away `_id` and produce exactly `order_id`, `total`, `customer_name`, and `tier`; use `$ifNull` so `customer_name` and `tier` are present with `null` when no customer matches. Then sort by `order_id` ascending.
3. Inspect the seeded collection counts with MongoDB's native client, then run the tests:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec -T mongo mongosh shop --quiet --eval 'printjson({customers: db.customers.countDocuments({}), orders: db.orders.countDocuments({})})'
   docker compose exec -T app python document_lookup.py
   ```

   Confirm that the native-client check reports 3 customers and 5 orders. Temporarily set `preserveNullAndEmptyArrays` to `false`, rerun the Python command, observe that the assertion detects the changed semantics, then restore `true`.
4. In 3–5 sentences, compare lookup-at-read-time with embedding a customer-name snapshot in every order. Address current customer names, historical invoice names, update cost, and read locality.
5. Tear down the Docker stack with `docker compose down -v`.
practice.answer:
```python
from __future__ import annotations

import os

from pymongo import MongoClient


MONGO_URL = os.environ["MONGO_URL"]
MONGO_DB = os.environ["MONGO_DB"]


def joined_orders(db) -> list[dict]:
    pipeline = [
        {"$match": {"status": "paid", "total": {"$gte": 50}}},
        {
            "$lookup": {
                "from": "customers",
                "localField": "customer_id",
                "foreignField": "_id",
                "as": "customer",
            }
        },
        {"$unwind": {"path": "$customer", "preserveNullAndEmptyArrays": True}},
        {
            "$project": {
                "_id": 0,
                "order_id": "$_id",
                "total": 1,
                "customer_name": {"$ifNull": ["$customer.name", None]},
                "tier": {"$ifNull": ["$customer.tier", None]},
            }
        },
        {"$sort": {"order_id": 1}},
    ]
    return list(db.orders.aggregate(pipeline))
```

Commands and results:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch3-p7 init
docker compose up -d --wait
ls -l
docker compose exec -T mongo mongosh shop --quiet --eval 'printjson({customers: db.customers.countDocuments({}), orders: db.orders.countDocuments({})})'
docker compose exec -T app python document_lookup.py
```

The native MongoDB check returned `{ customers: 3, orders: 5 }`. The Python test printed the expected rows: orders 1001, 1003, 1004, and unmatched order 1005 with `None` customer fields. With `preserveNullAndEmptyArrays` temporarily changed to `False`, order 1005 disappeared and the final shape assertion raised `AssertionError`; restoring `True` made the test pass again.

A lookup at read time shows the current customer name, since it joins against the current customer document. Embedding a customer-name snapshot in each order preserves the historical invoice name even if the customer later changes it. The embedded approach makes name changes expensive because every affected order must be updated, while lookup centralizes that update in one customer document. Embedded data also improves read locality because an order can be rendered without a join, whereas lookup trades that locality for current, normalized customer data.

```bash
docker compose down -v
```

practice.task: [RDFLib, SPARQL] Learn how RDF triples and graph queries model connected data.
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Python 3.10+ with `pip` and `venv` on macOS or Linux using a POSIX-compatible shell.

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv-ch3-rdf
source .venv-ch3-rdf/bin/activate
python -m pip install rdflib==7.6.0

# Confirm install
python -c 'import rdflib; assert rdflib.__version__ == "7.6.0", rdflib.__version__; print(rdflib.__version__)'
```

A triple store represents every fact as subject-predicate-object: for example, `myapp` is the subject, `dependsOn` is the predicate, and `logger` is the object. Load the same package graph used in the relational and graph-database exercise from Turtle RDF, then query it with SPARQL.

Save the following as `sparql_dependencies.py`. The RDF graph already contains package names, versions, types, and dependency edges; complete only the three SPARQL strings.

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from rdflib import Graph


DATA = """
@prefix ex: <https://example.test/package/> .
@prefix schema: <https://schema.org/> .

ex:myapp     a schema:SoftwareApplication; schema:name "myapp";     schema:softwareVersion "1.0.0"; ex:dependsOn ex:webserver, ex:logger .
ex:webserver a schema:SoftwareApplication; schema:name "webserver"; schema:softwareVersion "2.3.1"; ex:dependsOn ex:router, ex:logger .
ex:router    a schema:SoftwareApplication; schema:name "router";    schema:softwareVersion "1.4.0"; ex:dependsOn ex:http-lib, ex:crypto .
ex:http-lib  a schema:SoftwareApplication; schema:name "http-lib";  schema:softwareVersion "3.1.0" .
ex:logger    a schema:SoftwareApplication; schema:name "logger";    schema:softwareVersion "2.0.0"; ex:dependsOn ex:utils .
ex:utils     a schema:SoftwareApplication; schema:name "utils";     schema:softwareVersion "1.1.0" .
ex:crypto    a schema:SoftwareApplication; schema:name "crypto";    schema:softwareVersion "4.2.0" .
"""


DIRECT = """
PREFIX ex: <https://example.test/package/>
PREFIX schema: <https://schema.org/>
# TODO: direct dependency query
SELECT ?name ?version WHERE { BIND("" AS ?name) BIND("" AS ?version) FILTER(false) }
"""


TRANSITIVE = """
PREFIX ex: <https://example.test/package/>
PREFIX schema: <https://schema.org/>
# TODO: transitive dependency query
SELECT ?name ?version WHERE { BIND("" AS ?name) BIND("" AS ?version) FILTER(false) }
"""


REVERSE = """
PREFIX ex: <https://example.test/package/>
PREFIX schema: <https://schema.org/>
# TODO: reverse dependency query
SELECT ?name WHERE { BIND("" AS ?name) FILTER(false) }
"""


def values(graph: Graph, query: str) -> list[tuple[str, ...]]:
    return [tuple(str(value) for value in row) for row in graph.query(query)]


def main() -> None:
    graph = Graph().parse(data=DATA, format="turtle")
    direct = values(graph, DIRECT)
    transitive = values(graph, TRANSITIVE)
    reverse = values(graph, REVERSE)
    assert sorted(direct) == [("logger", "2.0.0"), ("webserver", "2.3.1")]
    assert sorted(transitive) == [
        ("crypto", "4.2.0"),
        ("http-lib", "3.1.0"),
        ("logger", "2.0.0"),
        ("router", "1.4.0"),
        ("utils", "1.1.0"),
        ("webserver", "2.3.1"),
    ]
    assert sorted(name for (name,) in reverse) == ["logger", "myapp", "webserver"]
    print("direct:", direct)
    print("transitive:", transitive)
    print("reverse:", reverse)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Tasks:
1. Complete `DIRECT` with a basic graph pattern matching `ex:myapp ex:dependsOn ?package`, then obtain each package's `schema:name` and `schema:softwareVersion`.
2. Complete `TRANSITIVE` using the SPARQL property path `ex:dependsOn+` and `SELECT DISTINCT` to find every package reachable by one or more dependency edges.
3. Complete `REVERSE` by placing `?package` at the start of a path ending at `ex:utils`, then return each package name.
4. In your written response, identify the subject, predicate, and object in one dependency triple. Explain why adding a new predicate such as `ex:license` needs no table migration, and note that the `+` property path finds reachability but does not directly report minimum hop count. This explanation requires no Python edits.
5. Run the tests:

   ```bash
   python sparql_dependencies.py
   ```
practice.answer:
```python
DIRECT = """
PREFIX ex: <https://example.test/package/>
PREFIX schema: <https://schema.org/>
SELECT ?name ?version WHERE {
    ex:myapp ex:dependsOn ?package .
    ?package schema:name ?name ; schema:softwareVersion ?version .
}
"""

TRANSITIVE = """
PREFIX ex: <https://example.test/package/>
PREFIX schema: <https://schema.org/>
SELECT DISTINCT ?name ?version WHERE {
    ex:myapp ex:dependsOn+ ?package .
    ?package schema:name ?name ; schema:softwareVersion ?version .
}
"""

REVERSE = """
PREFIX ex: <https://example.test/package/>
PREFIX schema: <https://schema.org/>
SELECT ?name WHERE {
    ?package ex:dependsOn+ ex:utils .
    ?package schema:name ?name .
}
"""
```

Run:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv-ch3-rdf
source .venv-ch3-rdf/bin/activate
python -m pip install rdflib==7.6.0
python -c 'import rdflib; assert rdflib.__version__ == "7.6.0", rdflib.__version__; print(rdflib.__version__)'
python sparql_dependencies.py
```

In the triple `ex:myapp ex:dependsOn ex:logger`, the subject is `ex:myapp`, the predicate is `ex:dependsOn`, and the object is `ex:logger`. RDF graphs are schema-flexible: adding a fact with a new predicate such as `ex:license` simply adds triples, so it does not require a relational table migration. The `ex:dependsOn+` property path finds packages reachable through one or more dependency edges, but it does not directly return the minimum hop count to each package.

practice.task: [PostgreSQL] Learn how to separate transactional and analytical workloads with a star-schema warehouse.
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop).

This lab runs a PostgreSQL retailer database with a preloaded OLTP source and an incomplete warehouse scaffold.

Setup:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch3-p9 init
docker run -d --name lab-ch3-p9 -p 5432:5432 ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch3-p9
```

A retailer runs checkout and analytics on one normalized PostgreSQL OLTP schema. Checkout needs fast point queries, while analysts run scans over order history. Build a separate star-schema warehouse for category-by-month and customer-country revenue reporting while keeping OLTP authoritative.

:::cut Review the warehouse scaffold
The image provisions the OLTP schema and source rows. The generated `setup.sql` contains only these warehouse edit sites:

```sql
-- implement: date dimension
-- CREATE TABLE warehouse.dim_date (...);

-- implement: customer dimension
-- CREATE TABLE warehouse.dim_customer (...);

-- implement: product dimension
-- CREATE TABLE warehouse.dim_product (...);

-- implement: order-line fact table
-- CREATE TABLE warehouse.fact_order_items (...);

-- implement: warehouse load
-- INSERT INTO warehouse.dim_date ...
-- INSERT INTO warehouse.dim_customer ...
-- INSERT INTO warehouse.dim_product ...
-- INSERT INTO warehouse.fact_order_items ...
```

```bash
ls -l setup.sql verify.sql
```

Expected lab files: `setup.sql` and `verify.sql`.
:::

Tasks:

1. Complete the four edit sites in `setup.sql`. Create `warehouse.dim_date` with `date_key`, `year`, and `month`; `warehouse.dim_customer` with `customer_key` and `country`; `warehouse.dim_product` with `product_key` and `category`; and `warehouse.fact_order_items` with at least the three dimension keys and `revenue`, with one row for every source `oltp.order_items` row. You may add a surrogate `fact_key`; if you add a fact key, do not assume that `(order_id, product_id)` uniquely identifies source order lines. Make the table DDL safe to reapply.
2. Implement the ETL load from `oltp` into all four warehouse tables with SQL `INSERT ... SELECT`. Derive `revenue` from the recorded order-line quantity and price. Make a repeated full load safe by clearing and rebuilding the derived warehouse data or by using idempotent upserts.
3. Apply the completed warehouse file twice to exercise the repeat-safe load:

   ```bash
   docker exec -i lab-ch3-p9 psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d retail_lab < setup.sql
   docker exec -i lab-ch3-p9 psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d retail_lab < setup.sql
   ```

4. Run the supplied verification test:

   ```bash
   docker exec -i lab-ch3-p9 psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d retail_lab < verify.sql
   ```

5. In short plain prose, state which schema is the system of record, which is derived data, and why analytical queries should use the warehouse rather than scanning `oltp`.
6. Tear down the Docker lab with `docker rm -f lab-ch3-p9`. In your solution write-up, include the completed `setup.sql` and a short run record confirming that Tasks 3, 4, and 6 completed successfully.
practice.answer:
Completed `setup.sql`:

```sql
-- setup.sql
-- implement: date dimension
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS warehouse.dim_date (
  date_key integer PRIMARY KEY,
  year integer NOT NULL,
  month integer NOT NULL
);

-- implement: customer dimension
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS warehouse.dim_customer (
  customer_key integer PRIMARY KEY,
  country text NOT NULL
);

-- implement: product dimension
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS warehouse.dim_product (
  product_key integer PRIMARY KEY,
  category text NOT NULL
);

-- implement: order-line fact table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS warehouse.fact_order_items (
  fact_key bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  date_key integer NOT NULL REFERENCES warehouse.dim_date(date_key),
  customer_key integer NOT NULL REFERENCES warehouse.dim_customer(customer_key),
  product_key integer NOT NULL REFERENCES warehouse.dim_product(product_key),
  revenue numeric NOT NULL
);

-- implement: warehouse load
TRUNCATE TABLE warehouse.fact_order_items, warehouse.dim_date,
  warehouse.dim_customer, warehouse.dim_product RESTART IDENTITY;

INSERT INTO warehouse.dim_date (date_key, year, month)
SELECT DISTINCT
  (EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.created_at)::integer * 10000
   + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM o.created_at)::integer * 100
   + EXTRACT(DAY FROM o.created_at)::integer),
  EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.created_at)::integer,
  EXTRACT(MONTH FROM o.created_at)::integer
FROM oltp.orders AS o;

INSERT INTO warehouse.dim_customer (customer_key, country)
SELECT c.id, c.country
FROM oltp.customers AS c;

INSERT INTO warehouse.dim_product (product_key, category)
SELECT p.id, p.category
FROM oltp.products AS p;

INSERT INTO warehouse.fact_order_items
  (date_key, customer_key, product_key, revenue)
SELECT
  (EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.created_at)::integer * 10000
   + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM o.created_at)::integer * 100
   + EXTRACT(DAY FROM o.created_at)::integer),
  o.customer_id,
  oi.product_id,
  oi.quantity * oi.price
FROM oltp.order_items AS oi
JOIN oltp.orders AS o ON o.id = oi.order_id;
```

`oltp` is the system of record: it remains authoritative for operational checkout data. `warehouse` is derived data rebuilt from `oltp`. Analytical queries should use the warehouse because its star schema has pre-joined, reporting-oriented dimensions and facts, avoiding repeated scans and joins over the normalized OLTP tables that support checkout.
